Quiet, please. Thank you. Good evening and welcome to the New York City Hybrid Hearing on the Committee on Women and Gender Equity, jointly with the Committee on Veterans. Please silence all electronic devices at this time. Also, please do not approach the dais. If you have any questions, please raise your hand. One of us, Sergeant at Arms, will kindly assist you. Chairs, we're ready to begin.

Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Frank Morano. Very, very pleased to welcome you to this hearing, which is very special. We'll get into all the reasons why. Particularly special for me, because this is my very first hearing that I'm chairing. As the new Chairman of the City Council Veterans Committee. I'd just like to say a word about that role and this committee, and then talk a little bit about the topic that we're going to explore today before welcoming the Commissioner and our Co-chair, Council Member Farías. I really am so

honored and privileged to be chairing this committee, and I can't thank Speaker Menin enough for this opportunity. And I'll just say to the public and to, you know, anybody watching either here or wherever, that I intend to make a very, very big splash with this committee. I intend to use this committee to help a lot of folks. I never served in the military myself, and I've always felt a bit guilty about that. Very— I've always been proud to be the grandson of a Purple Heart recipient, but I view this honestly as my way to give back and to really go to war with bureaucracy in order to help the people that have worn our nation's uniform and literally put their lives on the line for our freedom. And I'm looking forward to doing some very, very big things. Now a lot of the ways that different committee chairs work is you can get by relying on the great work that the committee staff does, and we do have a terrific committee staff with the Veterans Committee, Alejandro and Manur and the entire team at the Veterans Committee has done a yeoman's job, not only in preparation for this hearing, but everything the Veterans Committee does. They will research the topic, they'll suggest topics, they will even write

questions for witnesses that are in many cases much brighter than anything I could come up with. But I'll tell you, I have no intention while I'm holding this gavel of just being a plug-and-play committee chairman. I intend to drive this committee into a place where we're going to be a leading voice on veterans issues in the city, this region, and this country. I'm intending to come up with some great legislation that is going to improve the lives for the men and women that have served in uniform that live in this city. And they're facing a lot of challenges. We're going to hear about some of them today, and I am determined to make sure that we have a big impact for the next few years. This particular hearing is of great interest and great importance to me, because we're exploring the issue of how we can do a better job serving women veterans. Even though I'm not a woman, I am a lifelong fan of women, and as my wife and I are expecting a little girl in July, the subject has even more resonance for me. So I'm very, very excited to be here and to help a population that I don't think has gotten, the— what they deserve in terms of city services over the last few years. I’m looking forward to working with all

the members of the Veterans Committee, all of whom I know and have worked with before, all of whom are great advocates for the men and women that have served the military. Before I introduce and welcome the Commissioner, I also want to personally tell folks how privileged I am to be able to co-chair this particular hearing with Chairwoman Farías. When I met with her one-on-one for the first time, I told her, and it has the added virtue of being true, that she is exactly the type of council member and the type of leader in this body that I'd like to emulate. And while we may differ in terms of voting records and different opinions on things, I think you'd be hard-pressed to find a harder working and a better council member, and I couldn't think of a better chairperson person to learn from, from my first hearing. With that, I will give you Chairwoman Farías. CHAIRPERSON FARÍAS: As a lifelong fan of women myself, I'll say that—

[interposing] Enthusiastic— CHAIRPERSON FARÍAS: I'm a big fan of Chair Morano. Thank you so much for your kind words

and for chairing this hearing with me. Good afternoon, everyone. As mentioned, I'm Councilmember Amanda Farías, and I chair the Committee on Women and Gender Equity. And I'm proud to convene this joint oversight hearing with the Committee on Veterans on Serving Women Veterans today. I want to thank again Chair Morano for partnering on this really important conversation. I would like to also recognize committee members from Women and Gender Equity, Council Members Gutiérrez, Schulman, and Aldebol for joining us. Today's hearing is not just about numbers. It is about visibility, dignity, and responsibility. Women are the fastest growing population within the veteran community nationwide, and with more than 2 million women having served our country, here in New York City, we are home to one of the largest concentrations of women veterans in the country, approximately 12,800 women who wore the uniform and made the same oath to serve as their male counterparts. Yet despite their service, sacrifice, and leadership, women veterans continue to return home to systems that were not built with them in mind. As more women enter and advance through the ranks of our military, our post-service

infrastructure has not quite kept pace. The agency programs and cultural assumptions that shape veteran services were historically designed around the experiences of men. As a result, women veterans are too often navigating healthcare systems that do not fully address gender-specific needs, mental and behavioral health services that fail to account for trauma-informed care, housing systems that overlook safety considerations, and workforce pipelines that do not reflect their skill sets or lived experiences. We must also name what is often left unsaid: the compounded impact of racism, sexual discrimination, harassment, violence, heterosexism, and systemic bias. These realities shape the military experience for many women, particularly women of color, LGBTQ+ women, and immigrant women, and they do not disappear once service ends. If we are serious about equity, our policies must acknowledge and respond to those intersecting barriers. Nationally, one in three women veterans report experiencing military sexual trauma. Women veterans face disproportionately high rates of intimate partner violence, housing instability, and suicide compared to non-veteran women. Many report struggling to make ends meet despite having served

their country honorably. These are not isolated statistics. They are indicators of structural gaps and in care and in support. Women veterans deserved more than gratitude. They deserve systems that recognize the full scope of their service and meet them with competent, culturally responsive, and trauma-informed care. They deserve a transition from service member to veteran that affirms their identity, their health, their safety, and their economic security. Today's hearing is about accountability. It is about asking whether New York City is truly meeting this moment, how we're ensuring veterans are aware of and able to access the benefits they have earned, how are we addressing gender-specific healthcare and mental health needs, how are we protecting women veterans from homelessness and violence, and how are we collecting the data necessary to understand whether our interventions are actually working. There is clearly more work to be done, not only nationally but right here in New York City. It is also my distinct personal privilege to congratulate our newly appointed Commissioner of the New York City Department of Veterans Services, Yesenia Mata.

Commissioner Mata's appointment is a meaningful moment for our city, and I look forward to working closely with her to ensure that all veterans, especially women veterans, for today receive the respect, care, and resources they have earned through their service. Leadership matters, and I'm hopeful that under her stewardship, we will continue strengthening how New York City shows up for those who have served. I want to thank the members of the Committee on Women and Gender Equity who have joined us today, as well as our committee staff, Julia Goldsmith-Pinkham, Katie Salina, Taylor Francisco, and Ali Stauffer, and my own team, Dan Curtin and Josephine Kauras, for their preparation and commitment to this issue. And thank you again, Chair Morano, for your partnership. I look forward to a thoughtful and solutions-oriented discussion. I will now turn it back over to you.

Thank you, Chair Farías. I want to before we hear from our first folks, I want to pick up on what my colleague mentioned in terms of the importance of the topic we're exploring today. Women veterans represent one of the fastest-growing segments of the veterans

population, and for a long time, the experiences of women veterans haven't been fully reflected in policy discussions. And while a lot of the challenges they face are the same as what men are facing, many of them are specific to them, including access to gender-specific healthcare, mental health services, childcare, and protection from gender-based discrimination and harassment. And what I'm hoping is that this hearing is an opportunity to review what's working, see where gaps remain, and how agencies and community partners can better connect women veterans to services. And, also we can examine whether current outreach efforts are effective. Now, in addition to our oversight topic today, we are going to be hearing the following pieces of legislation, both of which I'm privileged to be a sponsor of, Reso Number 0014, sponsored by Council Member Joann Ariola, which would call upon the New York City Housing Authority to include an admission preference for public housing in its next proposed agency plan for for all veterans of the U.S. military, and Reso number 0131, sponsored by my colleague Council Member Paladino, which would call on the New York City Department of Education to observe Veterans Day the Friday before November 11th

if it falls on a Saturday, and the Monday after the 11th if it falls on a Sunday. Council Member Ariola is not able to join us this afternoon, but we certainly look forward to hearing and discussing her resolution. Let me invite my, colleague from Queens, Council Member Paladino, to speak about her resolution.

Thank you, Frank. Thank you, Chairman. Sorry. Anyway, good afternoon, everybody. It's a privilege to be here at the first Veterans Committee hearing. Being on the Veterans Committee for the last four years, starting my 5th year now, it was a pleasure to meet the Commissioner in my office the other day. We had a very productive conversation and much needed, and I look forward to a very good working relationship moving forward. This is indeed an extremely important topic, one that is overlooked and just taken for granted most all the time. So, get– to go to my Reso. The reso is kind of cute, because it was brought to my attention by the kids in my school districts. And how important— because I honor the veterans once a year in my office. We do a veterans breakfast, and you cannot believe— I have 27 schools, and out of

those 27 schools, they write the most phenomenal cards, and my vets take it away with them at every single breakfast. So one of which was, why can't we get the day off from school to acknowledge Veterans Day? If Veterans Day falls on a Saturday or a Sunday, It's so important what a veteran does. These are kids telling me this, mind you. These are grade school and middle school kids. And I said, you know what, you're right. And I said to my, chief let's put together legislation whereas we can honor our veterans should the holiday fall on a Saturday or Sunday. If the kids are smart enough to know how important Veterans Day is, well then, so should we be. So I'm looking forward to passing this Reso. Thank you very much, everybody.

Thank you, Council Member Paladino. I'm looking forward to today's testimony and to strengthening support for women veterans throughout New York City. I do want to acknowledge, my colleagues in addition to Council Member Paladino who are here today. From the Veterans Committee, you have Council Member Phil Wong. Hello, Council Member Wong. We have Council Member Carmen De La Rosa. And, I believe, Chair

Farías acknowledged them as well, but from our counterpart committee, we have Council Members Gutiérrez, Schulman, Aldebol, and joining us via Zoom, Council Member Santosuosso. Hello, everybody. Thank you, everybody, for being here. All right, before we get started, I do want to thank as well the incredible staff of the Veterans Committee. I mentioned a few folks before, but I don't want to omit every— anybody. I to thank our Legislative Counsel Alejandro Carvajal, our Policy Analyst Manur Butte, and Financial Analyst Margaret Barnsley for their work in preparing for this hearing. I'd also like to thank my entire staff for their work as we continue to serve our constituents and the city as a whole. With that, I'd like to turn it over to our Committee Counsel to administer the oath to witnesses from the administration.

Thank you, Chair. I'll call on you one by one. Please raise your right hands. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony before these committees, and to respond honestly to council members' questions? Commissioner Mata?
Yes, I do.
Deputy Commissioner Villarreal [sp?]? That's— could— would you mind stating your name? This is the slip we got.
Executive Director Donee Smalls.
Executive Director Smalls?
Yes.
Nicole Orlando?
I do.
Thank you. And as a reminder to all of our witnesses, please state your name prior to your testimony for the record.

Thank you, everybody. Before you begin your testimony, I do want to say a word about our brand new DVS Commissioner. For starters, I am a little irked because clearly we missed the memo to wear pink today, which is one of my favorite colors as a lifelong fan of women. But, I do wanna mention specifically that we're very, very excited to have a Commissioner and a Veterans Committee Chairperson that are both from the great borough of Staten Island. Staten Island often gets forgotten in terms of city services, and we have a

very large veterans population, and I think it says a lot about our priorities that we have two prominent veterans leaders, both from Staten Island. But about this Commissioner specifically, Commissioner Mata went out of her way to meet individually with every single member of the Veterans Committee, visiting each of them individually in their office. And I may be relatively new to the City Council, but I'm not new to being an observer of city government. That's a pretty rare thing for a brand new citywide Commissioner to do, and I think it says a great deal about her commitment to veterans in this city and her willingness to work with each of us on this committee, even though we may not necessarily see the world the same way. So, on behalf of Staten Islanders, Commissioner, and my fellow committee members, thank you very, very much. I'd love to hear your remarks.

Good morning, Chair Morano, Chair Farías, and members of the committees. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. My name is Yesenia Mata, and I have the honor of serving as Commissioner of the New York City Department of Veterans Services. I also have the honor of serving

as Captain in the United States Army Reserves. Today's hearing matters to me personally because it focuses on women veterans. I still remember when I first enlisted. I started as an enlisted soldier, became a sergeant, and later became a captain. In each rank, I try my best to support other women soldiers and veterans, because there are still not many of us in leadership ranks. I also want to acknowledge military spouses and children. They serve, too. I know that deeply as a military spouse myself and what it feels to be separated from your partner. Women veterans and military families do not all have the same story, but we share the same core truth: we served. And when a woman veteran is not seen or supported, it affects more than just her. It affects her family, too. That is a reality this hearing is confronting. Women's service is growing, yet women veterans are still too often overlooked in how systems identify them. Today, I want to offer an overview and what role the city can play alongside the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. More than 2.1 million women veterans live in the United States. 580,000 veterans live in New York State, about 131,000 in New York City, including 15,678 women

veterans. Research focused on New York shows two themes: our veteran population is more racially and ethnically diverse than the national average, and many veterans, especially women and minority veterans, report difficulty navigating the systems designed to serve them. And I'm going to repeat that number again. More than 2.1 million women veterans live in the United States. 580,000 veterans live in New York State and about 131,000 in New York City. And again, including 15,678 women veterans are vetted here and have registered here in New York City. Women are also the fastest growing group within the veteran population. That matters here in New York City where diversity is the norm and where support is spread across federal, state, and local systems that do not always feel connected from the resident's point of view. That is what I want to focus on today: visibility and how it affects access and outcomes. Often support starts with a simple question: have you served in the U.S. military? If that question is never asked or if it does not feel safe to answer, doors stay closed. When veterans do not self-identify, they are less likely to be connected to benefits and care they earned, and they are less

likely to be counted in systems that shape policy and funding. For women veterans, there is an added layer. They are making those decisions in a culture where the public image of a woman is still too often male by default. So, self-identification is not just a checkbox. If self-identification is a front door, the next question is why so many women veterans do not walk through it. One part of the answer is the handoff after service. Research shows that efforts to support women's transitions have too often been treated as a health-focused supplement rather than a whole-of-life handoff that accounts for the full realities of leaving services. There are a few common barriers we should keep in mind. First, not everyone sees themselves reflected in veteran messaging. Many women veterans describe not being recognized, including not being seen as real veterans in the way the public imagines military service to be. Second, practical barriers compound hours of operation, child care needs, privacy, and comfort in check-in and waiting spaces all affect whether someone follows through. Third, access is not just whether care exists, it is whether someone can actually reach it. Phone access matters, long holds, drop calls, and no

call box Callbacks can turn people away. And for many women veterans, access is all about trust. Nationally, VA screening data have long shown that about one in three women who use VA healthcare report experiencing military sexual trauma. That reality shapes how people approach this. Finally, for some women veterans, service is not something they want to narrate to strangers. That includes trauma. It also includes the simple reality that many people want to remove— want to move forward from their service, but life happens. Later, those same individuals may need healthcare benefits, housing stability, or help navigating systems. RAND has warned that the VA may still fall short in meeting women veterans' mental health needs, particularly for care related to combat trauma and military sexual trauma. The result is straightforward: when the path to support feels unclear, unwelcoming, or unsafe, people stop trying, and systems can confuse low utilization for low need. Where the VA fits: I have talked about what women veterans experience on the ground. I also want to briefly name the federal systems they depend on. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs is a primary federal agency responsible for veterans' healthcare

benefits such as disability compensation and pensions and cemeteries and memorial benefits. Over time, the VA has built more formal structures to address women veteran needs. For example, Congress established the Advisory Committee on Women Veterans in 1983 and created the Center for Women Veterans in 1994. Even with these improvements, participation in VA healthcare still shows a gap. In 2023, about 930,000 women veterans were enrolled in VA healthcare, and about 650,000 sought VA medical care. Those numbers tell a story. The system is serving many women and still not reaching many others. Enrollment and utilization are not the same. Getting someone enrolled does not automatically mean they are connected, comfortable, and consistently accessing care where the city agency fits. With that as a backdrop, I want to bring the focus back to what we can control at the city level. Our job is practical. We help women veterans move from eligibility to access, and we do it in a system where support is spread across federal, state, and local lanes that do not always feel connected from the resident's point of view. In 2025, DVS served 1,509 veterans across our core service areas. Of that total, we served 393

women veterans through housing stabilization, employment support, VA claims assistance, entrepreneurship services. The most common needs we see are benefits navigation, housing stability, and employment support. That aligns with New York-based research showing that navigating systems, especially for women and minority veterans, is often the biggest hurdle. Our role is to simplify that path. We connect veterans to the right federal, state, local resources, explain the process in plain language, and stay engaged with them. We do not assume women veterans will find us through traditional channels. We build pathways with other organizations that already have trust and credibility with women veterans, including Women Veterans in Columbia University, the National Association of Black Military Women, and the Women Veterans Alliance, and the Pink Berets. We also collaborate with city partners including the Mayor's Office to End Domestic and Gender-based Violence, Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities, and Health and Hospitals because women veterans needs are often intersectional and because safety, stability, and access care are connected. We also see clearly that women veterans

are not only seeking services, they are building enterprises and creating jobs through our BASA Veteran Entrepreneurship Program. 28 percent of winners across three cohorts are women, women veterans. Looking ahead, we are also monitoring federal development that may impact women veterans' access to reproductive healthcare because shifts at the federal level often show up first as confusion at the local level, and confusion is a barrier. And because many women veterans do not self-identify in the first place, the work begins even earlier. We have to help women veterans feel seen and included before they ever need us. What DVS does for women veterans: At DVS, we approach support for women veterans through a simple frame, Connect. We connect women veterans to the right place, including VA healthcare benefits assistance, mental health supports, housing navigation, and trusted community partners, with an emphasis on warm handoffs and clear next steps. Reduce barriers: some barriers are informational, some are logistical, and some are cultural. We try to reduce all three by explaining the systems plainly and meeting people where they are at. Respect lived experience: Women veterans are not

a monolith. They are diverse across race, ethnicity, age, era of service, family structure, disability status, and identity. Our job is not to force a single veteran's story. It is to make sure women veterans can access support without having to fit someone else's stereotype. What we are asking for at this stage, based on what we see every day, there are three areas where partnerships from the Council would make a real difference. First, normalize asking the question everywhere. Women veterans are not always going to volunteer their veteran status. Systems should ask respectfully and routinely in ways that feel safe and purposeful. Have you served in the US military? Making that question standard practice across city touchpoints. Second, help veterans understand who does what. When veterans do not understand the split between, uh, city navigation and federal provisions, they often think this is not for me, I will get it later, or do I want the hassle? Clarity is a form of access. We welcome opportunities to work with the City Council on materials and messaging that clearly explain what DVS does and what the VA does. And thirdly, support pathways that work in real life. Access is not just about eligibility,

it is about logistics. That means scheduling flexibility, child care support, privacy considerations, and phone access. These are the practical details that determine whether someone can actually use the care and benefits they earn. We ask the City Council to support policies and programs that take these real-world constraints seriously when designing services for women veterans. And now I will close with this: women veterans have always been here. Our responsibility now is to make sure women veterans do not have to fight a second battle at home just to get care, benefits, and support. That standard— the standard will start here today by making them visible. It continues with self-identification that feels safe and worthwhile, and it depends on coordination between the VA, the city, and trusted community partners. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. I look forward to continuing this work with the committees and answering any questions you may have.

Thank you, Commissioner. Well done. I'll invite my colleagues who have questions to ask you them in a moment. But you emphasize that support often begins with a simple

question: have you served in the U.S. military? Which specific city agencies currently ask that question as part of their intake process, and which don't? And is there a plan to standardize that question across city agencies?

So in 2024, there was a Local Law 37, Intro 1237, that was passed that makes agencies responsible to implement that question. It's a voluntary survey question. At DVS, that is one of the priorities that we're going to be focusing on this year to ensure that all city agencies ask this question.

You mentioned that many women veterans are not always recognized as veterans in the first place. From what you're seeing on the ground here in New York, where does that gap show up the most? Is it in healthcare? Is it in housing access? Is it in employment service? Or is it somewhere else?

It's actually all across. As I said in my testimony, there are 131,000 veterans in New York City, and only 15,678 women veterans in New York City have been identified. So that shows that at all city agencies, at all

services, that women veterans are not being self-identified.

For the public's edification, your agency occupies a very unique role because unlike, say, the Commissioner of the Police Department who can just tell the police what to do, or Commissioner of the Fire Department who can tell the firemen what to do, you're in a position where so much of the benefits that New York City veterans are dependent upon are either federal benefits or state benefits, and your agency has a very, very difficult role to play in that you have to almost be a steering committee for a lot of these folks and steering them to federal agencies or state agencies. How does DVS work with the Department of Veterans Affairs? We have a close relationship with the Department of Veterans Affairs. We make it very clear that at DVS we are not the provider, but we are the sole connector. And as a sole connector, we also make sure that all city agencies that we partner up, up with are familiar with veteran issues, such as when it comes to the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities, or when it comes to the Department of Aging, or in general when it comes to any other city agency, we make sure

that they are aware of what is happening at a federal level too. So that makes us the connector.

Is there any specific coordination that goes on with the VA in supporting women veterans, specifically? So as DVS, we are not responsible what the VA does. Again, we are the sole connector, but we do make them aware of what is happening on the ground, that there has to be a better support of self-identification. Again, we, we are doing the best that we can to ensure that we can stay in communication because it's alarming that only 15,678 women veterans have been identified in New York City. You pointed out that enrollment in VA services doesn't necessarily mean someone's actually accessing care. Do we have any sense here in New York City of how many women veterans are enrolled in VA services but not actively using them, and what the barriers tend to be in those cases? So I'm going to pass that question to my Deputy Chief of Staff Nicole, but before that what we are noticing is that in one of the services that we do provide, what is through the VA Claims Unit, when women veterans do come, they either are coming for disability or unemployment, but through that process, then we are

able to see that at times they are– they're coming for other services too, whether it is that they would like to be connected in the community or in their neighborhood, or even that they experienced some sort of sexual trauma and that they would like additional services and support. So that is– generally when people do connect with DVS, whether it's through the phone or through partnerships that we have, we not only ask them for the benefits, but we also give them the opportunity to let us know what other types of services they need because we want to make sure that they're supported holistically. So now I'll pass that question to my Deputy Chief.

So in regards to the number of women veterans— and thank you, Chair, for the question. In terms of the women veterans who are enrolled in VA healthcare or utilizing a VA benefit, it's a little bit harder to tell on the number who are actually in terms utilizing it because that definition is so fluid. Some can be enrolled in healthcare going to a VA hospital once a year, every six months, every week, versus those who may be using a VA educational benefit or maybe are enrolled in the hospital but use private healthcare. So there's less

specific numbers on how many are enrolled actively using it, because it's something that is always changing.

Two final questions for me, and then I'll invite any of my colleagues who have questions to have at it. But you spoke about practical barriers like childcare and scheduling. Have you seen any models either in New York or elsewhere where childcare or flexible scheduling has significantly increased women veterans' ability to access services?

Well, I do— well, currently with the, with the new mayor that we have, I know that childcare is one of his biggest factors that he wants to ensure that women are supported at all levels. We do know that when it comes to child care, that is something that when it comes to veteran issues, people or individuals feel that that's not an issue that us women care about, or women that are currently serving in the military.
